lesson.title: Faking the Local Directory: How ARP Spoofing Hijacks Traffic
lesson.summary: ARP spoofing abuses the fact that ARP has no authentication, letting an attacker on a local network trick other devices into sending traffic to the attacker's MAC address instead of its rightful owner.
lesson.body:
Recall how ARP works: on a local network, devices ultimately deliver frames using MAC addresses, but applications think in terms of IP addresses. ARP bridges that gap. When a device needs to reach an IP address on its own subnet, it broadcasts a request asking who owns that address, and the device that owns it replies with its MAC address. To avoid repeating this for every packet, each device keeps a local cache mapping IP addresses to MAC addresses.

That cache is exactly what ARP spoofing exploits. ARP was designed for small, physically trusted networks, so it has no built in way to verify that a reply is genuine. Any device on the local network can send an ARP reply, even one nobody asked for, and other devices will accept it and update their cache with whatever mapping it contains. This is the same underlying idea as a spoofing attack in general: forging an identity, in this case an IP to MAC mapping, to gain trust the attacker never earned.

Consider a concrete scenario on an office or home network with a victim laptop, an attacker's laptop, and the gateway router that connects the network to the internet. The attacker sends the victim a forged ARP reply claiming the gateway's IP address now maps to the attacker's MAC address, and separately sends the gateway a forged reply claiming the victim's IP address now maps to the attacker's MAC address. From that point on, every packet the victim addresses to the gateway is actually delivered to the attacker's machine at the link layer, and every reply the gateway sends back to the victim goes to the attacker first. As long as the attacker quietly forwards the traffic along to its real destination, both the victim and the gateway keep functioning normally and notice nothing wrong, while the attacker sits in the middle able to read, and potentially alter, everything passing through. This is a classic man in the middle position, achieved without touching a single cable or breaking any password, just by lying to two devices about who owns which address.

It is worth being precise about the scope of this attack. ARP packets are never routed beyond the local subnet, so ARP spoofing only works when the attacker is already on the same local network segment as the victim, whether that is a shared office LAN or the same Wi-Fi access point. That local scope is what sets it apart from the next attack we will look at, DNS cache poisoning, which can redirect victims who are nowhere near the attacker at all. It is also worth noting that ARP spoofing intercepts traffic, but it does not automatically expose the contents of that traffic if the traffic itself is encrypted, a point that becomes important once we get to defense in depth and zero trust networking later in this unit.
